title: A Tensor Restriction Theorem over Finite Fields: reduction of Noetherianity for polynomial representations to the prime-field case (Proposition 4.5.1)
author: Andreas Blatter, Jan Draisma, Filip Rupniewski
work: A Tensor Restriction Theorem over Finite Fields
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Proposition 4.5.1 (source0.tex lines 1687--1691, source label prop:PrimeField), "Suppose that Theorem Noetherianity holds when $K$ is a prime field. Then it also holds when $K$ is an arbitrary finite field", delivered with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 1693--1715 (23 lines, one adjacent proof environment that opens and closes inside the retained span). The proposition is the pivot of the article's proof of its main Noetherianity theorem: the paper immediately records in a boxed remark (retained, lines 1717--1723) that "In view of Proposition~\ref{prop:PrimeField}, from now on we assume that $K$ is a prime field", and the rest of the proof of Noetherianity (the embedding theorem and the shift theorem, sections 4.6--4.8) is carried out only under that assumption. The author proof is complete and self-contained: it passes from the finite field $K$ to its prime field $F$ by restriction of scalars ($e:=\dim_F K$, $U_F$ the same abelian group as an $F$-vector space of dimension $e\dim_K U$), builds the generic representation $P_F(U):=(P(K\otimes_F U))_F$ over $F$ of the same degree as $P$, transports a descending chain $X_1\supseteq X_2\supseteq\ldots$ of subsets of $P$ to the chain $(X_1)_F\supseteq(X_2)_F\supseteq\ldots$ of subsets of $P_F$, applies the assumed prime-field statement, and concludes by evaluating at every $K^m$ that $X_n=X_{n_0}$ for $n\ge n_0$. That comparison of $X_n(K^m)$ with $(X_n)_F(F^m)$ through the identification $K^m=K\otimes_F F^m$, and the fact that a subset of a polynomial representation is determined by its values on the spaces $K^m$, are the substantive steps; they are short but they are not an exercise in unpacking definitions, and the proposition as stated is exactly the reduction on which a research proof of the main theorem rests. H2: a complete original research-paper proposition, moderately short, whose argument is a genuine restriction-of-scalars construction rather than a routine verification.
